title: Stargrove Retail on‑prem migration, rollback guidance, and Terraform advisory
body:
Purpose and scope:
This note captures a customer‑specific proposal for Stargrove Retail to run Redwood Private (on‑prem VPC) for production inference. It focuses on sizing assumptions, an upgrade/migration P0 plan with explicit rollback guidance, and pragmatic Terraform module notes for the delivery team. This is an internal advisory doc — not yet customer‑facing.

Context and target SLA:
- Customer: Stargrove Retail — single AWS Outposts footprint (primary), DR in a colocation rack in a second region.
- Target latency: 95th <= 80ms for 2k daily concurrent API connections (chat-style, avg prompt 120 tokens, completion 150 tokens).
- Throughput: steady 2.5 rps sustained per tenant peak, burst to 40 rps for flash promotions.
- Availability target: 99.9% monthly.

Key assumptions (call these out in customer kickoff):
1) Workload mix: 70% streaming chat (low-latency), 20% batch embeddings, 10% evals/longforms.
2) Model selection: internal plan to serve a 7B LLAMA-derivative quantized to 4-bit (q8-ish paths) and a 13B fallback.
3) KV cache hit expected: 18% prefix reuse on average (from telemetry) which influences batching and memory usage.
4) Network: private VPC with dedicated egress NAT; Stargrove will provide VLANs and allow RDMA inside cluster fabric.
5) Security: KMS available (customer-managed with HSM).

Proposed architecture (high level):
- Control plane: Redwood managed control plane (SaaS) with control channel over customer VPN.
- Data plane: On‑prem cluster (Outpost primary) running Redwood Private runtime inside k8s (EKS‑Anywhere/managed k8s node pool).
- GPU nodes: 3 x GPU nodes (each: 4 x A10G or 2 x A100‑40GB depending on procurement) for inference pool + 1 infra node for metrics/sidecars.
- Embedding workers: 2 x CPU‑heavy nodes with AVX512 and 512GB RAM for batched embeddings/ANN indexing (Faiss/HNSW).
- Networking: Calico CNI with IP‑per‑pod, MetalLB for LB, and local NVLink/RDMA where supported.
- Observability: Prometheus + Loki + opentelemetry collector shipping to a customer‑managed observability endpoint; retention 30d by default.

Sizing rationale and numbers (back‑of‑envelope):
- Baseline QPS requirement: 2.5 rps sustained => concurrency target (token generation latency/throughput) => estimate per‑request GPU time of 0.6s (7B quant). Concurrency band ~2.5*0.6 = 1.5 GPUs worth at baseline.
- Peak headroom for bursts and model fallback: target 4 GPUs available for inference. With node choices above: 3 nodes with 4 A10G each gives 12 A10G slots (approximated), enough to run multiple model shards and provide headroom for autoscaling.
- Memory and KV cache: each worker reserves 40–60GB for model weights + 12–20GB for KV cache. Total host RAM per GPU node target >= 256GB.

Terraform module notes and delivery checklist (actionable for infra eng):
- Modules to use: modules/cluster (k8s cluster), modules/gpu-node-pool, modules/networking/vpc-edge, modules/redwood-private-runtime.
- Provider versions: terraform >= 1.5, aws provider pinned at ~4.70.x for Outposts support. Document in PR.
- Required variables (canonical):
  - var.cluster_name (string)
  - var.region (string)
  - var.gpu_node_count (number)
  - var.gpu_instance_type (string)
  - var.kms_key_arn (string)
  - var.control_plane_endpoint (string)
- Important module behaviors/notes:
  - The gpu-node-pool module must expose a taint/label toggle 'redwood.inference/maintenance' to allow rolling drains.
  - Use lifecycle.ignore_changes for autoscaling_group.desired_capacity to allow Redwood operator to scale within bounds.
  - networking/vpc-edge should create NAT gateways in private subnets for software updates but optionally allow customer to manage NAT (flag: preserve_customer_nat = true).
- State and import: existing customer VPC subnets must be imported prior to apply. Use terraform import aws_vpc.vpc <vpc-id> and document exact resource ids in ticket JIRA-ENG-1428.
- Secrets: KMS keys must be created by customer and ARNs provided. Do NOT store raw keys in tfstate — enable state encryption with S3 SSE + DynamoDB locking.

Upgrade and migration plan (phased) with rollback safety:
Phase 0 — Prep (2 weeks)
- Deliverables: Terraform modules with defaults, inventory of customer network ranges, KMS ARNs, procurement lead time for GPUs.
- Validation: test cluster spin up in customer staging (small footprint).

Phase 1 — Staging validation (1 week)
- Deploy full stack to staging Outpost (1 GPU node) and run Redwood e2e smoke suite with sample traffic.
- Validate model load/unload, KV cache, and telemetry.
- Acceptance criteria: 95% of smoke tests pass, <10% request error budget on synthetic tests.

Phase 2 — Canary (48–72h)
- Canary route 3% production traffic to on‑prem cluster via smart routing. Monitor latency, error rates, and cost per token.
- Autoscale bounds: set min=1, max=6 GPUs for canary; set quick failover policy to hosted API if errors spike.
- Metrics to watch: 95th latency, request errors per minute, OOM/kube restarts, control plane heartbeats.

Phase 3 — Ramp and cutover (1–2 weeks)
- Gradually increase traffic to 50% then full production if no regressions. Keep hosted fallback enabled for 7 days.

Rollback guidance (explicit steps):
- Immediate rollback trigger: sustained error rate >2% for 30m or latency regression >2x baseline for 15m.
- Rollback mechanism: update routing policy in control plane to direct all traffic to hosted API (one button in Console). Then scale down on‑prem to min nodes.
- State rollback: do NOT revert tfstate unless absolutely required. Prefer runtime routing rollback + node drain. If TF rollback needed, create a new TF plan that sets node_count back to previous and apply; never directly edit state.

Operational runbooks and hardening notes:
- OOM mitigation: enable memory headroom env var to reduce batch sizes automatically when host memory pressure is high.
- Kernel/driver upgrades: schedule during maintenance window; require full node drain. Keep driver and CUDA versions pinned to runtime compatibility matrix; we recommend COS‑like distros for simpler GPU driver lifecycle.
- Monitoring: instrument token‑level spend and per‑route latency; set alert thresholds at 95th latency 120ms and error rate >0.5%.

Open questions for customer and engineering (to be resolved in kickoff):
- Does Stargrove want Redwood to manage KMS keys (via a gateway) or provide dedicated HSM? (impact on signing and export control)
- Procurement: prefer A10G vs A100-40? A100 saves memory headroom for larger models but has longer procurement lead time.
- DR strategy: Are hot cold standby nodes acceptable in DR region or do they require active sync?
- Network constraints: can the customer enable RDMA and allow intra-rack multicast for efficient KV cache sharing?

Acceptance criteria for GA handoff:
- Successful canary for 72h with no alert breaches.
- Documented TF modules in customer repo with integration tests (terraform-aws-integration pipeline passing).
- Runbook checklist complete and signed off by SRE and customer infra contact.

Immediate next steps and owners:
- Anita: finalize TF variable spec and open PR for modules (target: 2025-02-27).
- Diego: schedule staging Outpost window with customer (target: 2025-03-05).
- Priya: confirm KMS/HSM requirements and draft key rotation policy (target: 2025-02-28).
- Omar/Sam: prepare canary dashboard template and alerting rules.

Appendix — short terraform snippet examples (illustrative):
- Example: node pool invocation
module "gpu_node_pool" {
  source = "git::https://github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules.git//modules/gpu-node-pool"
  cluster_name = var.cluster_name
  gpu_instance_type = var.gpu_instance_type
  gpu_node_count = var.gpu_node_count
  labels = { "redwood.inference/role" = "runtime" }
}

- Example: lifecycle and ignore_changes for autoscaler
resource "aws_autoscaling_group" "gpu_asg" {
  # ...
  lifecycle {
    ignore_changes = [desired_capacity]
  }
}

Notes on uniqueness/known tradeoffs:
- We bias procurement towards more, smaller GPUs (A10G) to improve shard density and reduce OOM vs fewer, larger A100s which give single‑model performance but less granularity for multi‑tenant noisy neighbour control.
- Customer control plane connectivity: reliance on SaaS control plane requires network reachability and a small surface for outages — always document and test fallback flows.

If reviewers want, I can split this doc into: 1) Terraform PR checklist, 2) Runbook + rollback SOP, 3) Customer‑facing one‑pager.
